claim: Visual speed is believed to be underestimated at low contrast.
source_text: Visual speed is believed to be underestimated at low contrast, which has been proposed as an explanation of excessive driving speed in fog.
evidence_reasoning: This represents established belief in the field based on prior research, as indicated by the phrase 'is believed' and later citations to Thompson (1982), Stone and Thompson (1992), and others.

claim: Speed underestimation at low contrast has been proposed as an explanation of excessive driving speed in fog.
source_text: Visual speed is believed to be underestimated at low contrast, which has been proposed as an explanation of excessive driving speed in fog.
evidence_reasoning: This is a claim about what has been proposed in prior literature, as evidenced by later citations to Snowden et al. (1998), Horswill and Plooy (2008), and Owens et al. (2010).

claim: Speed is underestimated when contrast is reduced uniformly for all objects of the visual scene independently of their distance from the viewer.
source_text: we confirm that speed is underestimated when contrast is reduced uniformly for all objects of the visual scene independently of their distance from the viewer.
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study, specifically from experiments 1 and 2 showing speed underestimation with uniform contrast reduction.

claim: When contrast is reduced more for distant objects, as is the case in real fog, visual speed is actually overestimated.
source_text: However, we show that when contrast is reduced more for distant objects, as is the case in real fog, visual speed is actually overestimated, prompting drivers to decelerate.
evidence_reasoning: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from experiments 1 and 2 with distance-dependent contrast reduction.

claim: Speed overestimation in fog prompts drivers to decelerate.
source_text: when contrast is reduced more for distant objects, as is the case in real fog, visual speed is actually overestimated, prompting drivers to decelerate.
evidence_reasoning: This behavioral outcome is supported by data from experiment 2 showing that drivers drove slower in fog conditions.

claim: Perceived speed depends on the spatial distribution of contrast over the visual scene rather than the global level of contrast per se.
source_text: we demonstrate for the first time that perceived speed depends on the spatial distribution of contrast over the visual scene rather than the global level of contrast per se.
evidence_reasoning: This is a primary conclusion supported by data from all four experiments, particularly experiments 3 and 4 with anti-fog conditions.

claim: Visual contrast is usually referred to as the difference in brightness between an object and the background.
source_text: Visual contrast is usually referred to as the difference in brightness between an object and the background (Hofstetter et al., 2000).
evidence_reasoning: This is a definitional claim supported by citation to Hofstetter et al. (2000) and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Classical vision research experiments have shown that the perceived speed of two-dimensional moving objects is underestimated when visual contrast is reduced.
source_text: These studies have shown that the perceived speed of two-dimensional moving objects—for example, plaid patterns on a computer screen—is underestimated when visual contrast is reduced.
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by citations to Thompson (1982), Stone and Thompson (1992), Blakemore and Snowden (1999), and Anstis (2003).

claim: Recent studies based on driving scenarios have suggested that the underestimation of visual speed at low contrast applies also to perceived self-motion in three-dimensional environments.
source_text: More recent studies based on driving scenarios have suggested that the underestimation of visual speed at low contrast applies also to perceived self-motion in three-dimensional environments (Snowden et al., 1998; Horswill and Plooy, 2008; Owens et al., 2010).
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by citations to Snowden et al. (1998), Horswill and Plooy (2008), and Owens et al. (2010).

claim: Speed underestimation at low contrast was proposed and is still considered as a possible explanation for excessive driving speed in fog.
source_text: This finding was proposed—and is still considered—as a possible explanation for excessive driving speed in fog.
evidence_reasoning: This represents the current state of belief in the field based on prior research, as indicated by the citations and the phrase 'is still considered'.

claim: In all studies having assessed the effect of visual contrast on motion perception, contrast was reduced uniformly for all objects of the visual scene, irrespective of their distance from the observer.
source_text: In the abovementioned studies, and more generally in all studies having assessed the effect of visual contrast on motion perception, contrast was reduced uniformly for all objects of the visual scene, irrespective of their distance from the observer.
evidence_reasoning: This is a characterization of prior research methodology based on the cited studies and general knowledge of the field.

claim: Uniform contrast reduction is a valid model to assess the perception of two-dimensional patterns moving on a computer screen.
source_text: While uniform contrast reduction is a valid model to assess the perception of two-dimensional patterns moving on a computer screen, it is a poor model to investigate how an atmospheric phenomenon like fog affects motion perception in three-dimensional environments.
evidence_reasoning: This is an evaluative claim based on logical inference about the appropriateness of different experimental models for different contexts.

claim: Uniform contrast reduction is a poor model to investigate how an atmospheric phenomenon like fog affects motion perception in three-dimensional environments.
source_text: While uniform contrast reduction is a valid model to assess the perception of two-dimensional patterns moving on a computer screen, it is a poor model to investigate how an atmospheric phenomenon like fog affects motion perception in three-dimensional environments.
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing different effects of uniform vs. distance-dependent contrast reduction, and by logical inference about ecological validity.

claim: Fog alters visual contrast because tiny water droplets suspended in the air are interposed between the observer and the surrounding objects.
source_text: Specifically, fog alters visual contrast because tiny water droplets suspended in the air are interposed between the observer and the surrounding objects.
evidence_reasoning: This is a claim about the physical mechanism of fog based on established scientific knowledge about atmospheric phenomena.

claim: The quantity of water droplets in fog increases along the line-of-sight as distance from the observer increases.
source_text: The quantity of droplets increases along the line-of-sight as distance from the observer increases.
evidence_reasoning: This is a claim about the physical properties of fog based on established knowledge of atmospheric physics.

claim: In fog, the contrast of the visual scene decreases with distance.
source_text: As a consequence, the contrast of the visual scene decreases with distance, and visibility is better for close than for distant objects.
evidence_reasoning: This follows logically from the physical properties of fog and represents established knowledge about how fog affects visibility.

claim: In fog, visibility is better for close than for distant objects.
source_text: As a consequence, the contrast of the visual scene decreases with distance, and visibility is better for close than for distant objects.
evidence_reasoning: This is a direct consequence of the distance-dependent nature of fog and represents established knowledge.

claim: The distance-dependent attenuation of contrast experienced in fog is very different from the uniform reduction traditionally adopted in vision research.
source_text: Therefore, the distance-dependent attenuation of contrast experienced in fog is obviously very different from the uniform reduction traditionally adopted in vision research.
evidence_reasoning: This is a comparative claim based on logical inference from the different characteristics of the two types of contrast reduction.

claim: Uniform contrast reduction resembles more closely what one could experience when looking at the environment through a dirty glass or a foggy windshield.
source_text: Uniform contrast reduction resembles more closely what one could experience when looking at the environment through a dirty glass or a foggy windshield.
evidence_reasoning: This is an analogical claim based on logical inference about the visual effects of different types of visual obstruction.

claim: The effects of distance-dependent contrast reduction on motion perception are unknown.
source_text: To date, the effects of distance-dependent contrast reduction on motion perception are unknown.
evidence_reasoning: This is a claim about the state of knowledge in the field prior to this study, based on review of existing literature.

claim: We still do not know how fog affects perceived self-motion.
source_text: In other words, we still do not know how fog affects perceived self-motion.
evidence_reasoning: This restates the gap in knowledge identified in the field prior to this study.

claim: Twelve experienced drivers were presented with pairs of driving scenes in the first experiment.
source_text: Twelve experienced drivers were presented with pairs of driving scenes and instructed to estimate which scene moved faster
evidence_reasoning: This is a methodological fact about the experimental design and participant sample.

claim: Reducing the contrast of the visual scene altered speed perception with F(4,44) = 28.82, p<0.001, ηG2 = 0.42.
source_text: Reducing the contrast of the visual scene altered speed perception [F(4,44) = 28.82, p<0.001, ηG2 = 0.42].
evidence_reasoning: This is a statistical result from experiment 1 showing a significant main effect of contrast reduction on speed perception.

claim: The direction of the effect of contrast reduction on speed perception depended on the type of contrast reduction.
source_text: However, the direction of the effect depended on the type of contrast reduction.
evidence_reasoning: This is a finding from experiment 1 supported by the interaction between contrast type and perceived speed.

claim: As compared to clear visibility, speed was overestimated with distance-dependent visibility reduction (fog).
source_text: As compared to clear visibility (brown dashed line), speed was overestimated with distance-dependent visibility reduction (red bars)
evidence_reasoning: This is a primary finding from experiment 1 supported by PSE measurements showing speed overestimation in fog conditions.

claim: As compared to clear visibility, speed was underestimated with distance-independent visibility reduction (uniform contrast).
source_text: As compared to clear visibility (brown dashed line), speed was overestimated with distance-dependent visibility reduction (red bars) and underestimated with distance-independent visibility reduction (green bars).
evidence_reasoning: This is a primary finding from experiment 1 supported by PSE measurements showing speed underestimation with uniform contrast reduction.

claim: Reducing visibility affected speed discrimination sensitivity with F(4,44) = 29.58, p<0.001, ηG2 = 0.37.
source_text: Reducing visibility also affected speed discrimination sensitivity [F(4,44) = 29.58, p<0.001, ηG2 = 0.37]
evidence_reasoning: This is a statistical result from experiment 1 showing a significant effect of visibility reduction on discrimination sensitivity (JND).

claim: Speed discrimination sensitivity was significantly lower (higher JNDs) in the two conditions in which visibility was reduced in a distance-independent manner.
source_text: which was significantly lower (higher JNDs) in the two conditions in which visibility was reduced in a distance-independent manner (mean = 0.58 km/hr for both moderate and severe uniform reduction), as compared to the other three conditions that did not differ from one another (mean = 0.41, 0.40, and 0.42 km/hr for clear, moderate, and severe fog, respectively).
evidence_reasoning: This is a finding from experiment 1 supported by JND measurements comparing different visibility conditions.

claim: Participants had more difficulties estimating the driving speed when visibility reduction was independent of distance.
source_text: This indicates that the participants had more difficulties estimating the driving speed when visibility reduction was independent of distance.
evidence_reasoning: This is an interpretation of the JND data, inferring difficulty from higher discrimination thresholds.

claim: The reduction of speed discrimination sensitivity with uniform contrast might result from the fact that distance-independent contrast alteration is seldom encountered in real life.
source_text: This reduction of speed discrimination sensitivity might result from the fact that distance-independent contrast alteration is seldom encountered in real life.
evidence_reasoning: This is a speculative explanation for the observed pattern of results, as indicated by the word 'might'.

claim: Drivers usually demist their windshield before starting to drive.
source_text: Specifically, although entering a car with a foggy windshield is common, especially due to cold weather, drivers usually demist their windshield before starting to drive.
evidence_reasoning: This is a claim about common driving behavior based on general knowledge of driving practices.

claim: Drivers' options to reduce environmental fog are much more restricted than options to demist a windshield.
source_text: Unfortunately, drivers' options to reduce environmental fog are much more restricted.
evidence_reasoning: This is a claim based on general knowledge about the controllability of different visibility conditions.

claim: Ten experienced drivers who did not participate in the first experiment were tested in the second experiment.
source_text: Ten experienced drivers who did not participate in the first experiment were instructed to drive at target speeds with either clear or reduced visibility.
evidence_reasoning: This is a methodological fact about the experimental design and participant sample for experiment 2.

claim: Driving speed was affected by the contrast of the visual scene with F(4,36) = 43.18, p<0.001, ηG2 = 0.44.
source_text: Driving speed was affected by the contrast of the visual scene [F(4,36) = 43.18, p<0.001, ηG2 = 0.44].
evidence_reasoning: This is a statistical result from experiment 2 showing a significant main effect of contrast on driving speed.

claim: The direction of the effect of contrast on driving speed depended on the type of contrast reduction.
source_text: However, as for perceived speed, the direction of the effect depended on the type of contrast reduction.
evidence_reasoning: This is a finding from experiment 2 showing that the effect of contrast on driving behavior varied by contrast type.

claim: As compared to clear visibility, participants drove significantly slower with distance-dependent contrast reduction (fog).
source_text: As compared to clear visibility (mean = 85.1 km/hr), the participants drove significantly slower with distance-dependent contrast reduction (mean = 77.3 and 70.9 km/hr for moderate and severe fog, respectively)
evidence_reasoning: This is a primary finding from experiment 2 supported by measured driving speeds in different visibility conditions.

claim: As compared to clear visibility, participants drove faster with distance-independent reduction (uniform contrast).
source_text: but faster with distance-independent reduction (mean = 93.6 and 101.3 km/hr for moderate and severe uniform reduction, respectively
evidence_reasoning: This is a primary finding from experiment 2 supported by measured driving speeds in uniform contrast conditions.

claim: The five visibility conditions differed significantly from one another (p<0.05) in their effect on driving speed.
source_text: The five visibility conditions differed significantly from one another (p<0.05), and the same pattern was observed for all three target speeds.
evidence_reasoning: This is a statistical result from post-hoc tests in experiment 2.

claim: The same pattern of driving speed effects was observed for all three target speeds.
source_text: The five visibility conditions differed significantly from one another (p<0.05), and the same pattern was observed for all three target speeds.
evidence_reasoning: This indicates consistency of the effect across different speed conditions in experiment 2.

claim: Distance-dependent contrast reduction induces an overestimation of visual speed that prompts drivers to drive slower.
source_text: These behavioural results are consistent with the perceptual results of the first experiment and can be interpreted as follows: distance-dependent contrast reduction induces an overestimation of visual speed that prompts drivers to drive slower
evidence_reasoning: This is an interpretation linking the perceptual findings from experiment 1 with the behavioral findings from experiment 2.

claim: Distance-independent contrast reduction evokes an underestimation of visual speed, prompting drivers to drive faster.
source_text: whereas distance-independent contrast reduction evokes an underestimation of visual speed, prompting drivers to drive faster.
evidence_reasoning: This is an interpretation linking the perceptual findings from experiment 1 with the behavioral findings from experiment 2.

claim: The distance-dependent contrast reduction experienced in fog evokes perceptual and behavioural effects that are radically opposite to those resulting from the distance-independent contrast reduction traditionally adopted in vision research.
source_text: The results of the first two experiments highlight that the distance-dependent contrast reduction experienced in fog evokes perceptual and behavioural effects that are radically opposite to those resulting from the distance-independent contrast reduction traditionally adopted in vision research.
evidence_reasoning: This is a summary conclusion based on the contrasting results from experiments 1 and 2 for the two types of contrast reduction.

claim: In the experiments, the two types of contrast reduction resulted in the same global attenuation of visual contrast.
source_text: Such a radical difference is striking because in our experiments, the two types of contrast reduction resulted in the same global attenuation of visual contrast.
evidence_reasoning: This is a methodological fact about the experimental design, confirmed by the RMS contrast measurements reported in the methods.

claim: The global level of contrast is not the only factor affecting perceived speed.
source_text: This suggests that the global level of contrast is not the only factor affecting perceived speed.
evidence_reasoning: This is an inference drawn from the finding that identical global contrast levels produced opposite perceptual effects depending on spatial distribution.

claim: The spatial distribution of contrast over the visual scene plays a critical role in perceived speed.
source_text: The spatial distribution of contrast over the visual scene also seems to play a critical role.
evidence_reasoning: This is an inference from the differential effects of uniform vs. distance-dependent contrast reduction despite equal global contrast.

claim: In fog, when the driver looks straight ahead, the regions of better visibility in the proximity of the vehicle are typically viewed in peripheral vision.
source_text: Therefore, when the driver looks straight ahead, the regions of better visibility in the proximity of the vehicle are typically viewed in peripheral vision
evidence_reasoning: This is a logical inference about the spatial mapping of fog visibility onto the visual field based on the geometry of driving and fog properties.

claim: In fog, when the driver looks straight ahead, the distant regions where visibility is impaired fall in the centre of the driver's visual field.
source_text: whereas the distant regions where visibility is impaired fall in the centre of the driver's visual field (Snowden and Freeman, 2004).
evidence_reasoning: This is a logical inference about the spatial mapping of fog visibility onto the visual field, supported by citation to Snowden and Freeman (2004).

claim: In fog, fog acts as a mask obscuring the central region of the visual field.
source_text: In this situation, fog acts as a mask obscuring the central region of the visual field.
evidence_reasoning: This is a characterization of fog's effect based on logical inference from its distance-dependent properties and visual field mapping.

claim: Speed perception strongly depends on the visible portion of the visual field.
source_text: Recently, we have shown that speed perception strongly depends on the visible portion of the visual field (Pretto et al., 2009).
evidence_reasoning: This is a claim about prior research findings by the authors, supported by citation to Pretto et al. (2009).

claim: Speed is overestimated when the central area of the visual field is occluded.
source_text: In particular, we found that speed is overestimated when the central area is occluded, and underestimated when it is the peripheral area that is masked.
evidence_reasoning: This is a claim about prior research findings by the authors, supported by citation to Pretto et al. (2009).

claim: Speed is underestimated when the peripheral area of the visual field is masked.
source_text: In particular, we found that speed is overestimated when the central area is occluded, and underestimated when it is the peripheral area that is masked.
evidence_reasoning: This is a claim about prior research findings by the authors, supported by citation to Pretto et al. (2009).

claim: A similar phenomenon could explain why speed is overestimated in fog.
source_text: A similar phenomenon could explain why speed is overestimated in fog, that is, when contrast is reduced in a distance-dependent manner.
evidence_reasoning: This is a speculative hypothesis connecting prior findings to the current results, as indicated by 'could explain'.

claim: Speed overestimation in fog could result from the relative contrast between the central and peripheral areas of the visual field.
source_text: More specifically, speed overestimation in fog could result from the relative contrast between the central and peripheral areas of the visual field.
evidence_reasoning: This is a speculative mechanistic hypothesis, as indicated by 'could result from'.

claim: With anti-fog, visibility was better for distant than for close objects.
source_text: With anti-fog, visibility was better for distant than for close objects, that is, visibility was good for the portion of road situated at a distance ahead, and poor for the direct surroundings of the vehicle.
evidence_reasoning: This is a description of the anti-fog experimental condition created by the researchers.

claim: Normal fog and anti-fog resulted in opposite spatial distributions of contrast over the visual scene.
source_text: In other words, normal fog and anti-fog resulted in opposite spatial distributions of contrast over the visual scene, although the global contrast reduction was the same for both fog types.
evidence_reasoning: This is a methodological fact about the experimental design comparing fog and anti-fog conditions.

claim: The global contrast reduction was the same for both fog and anti-fog.
source_text: In other words, normal fog and anti-fog resulted in opposite spatial distributions of contrast over the visual scene, although the global contrast reduction was the same for both fog types.
evidence_reasoning: This is a methodological fact about the experimental design, confirmed by RMS contrast measurements.

claim: If the relative contrast between central and peripheral areas of the visual field underlies the speed overestimation observed with fog, then speed should be underestimated with the anti-fog.
source_text: We hypothesized that if the relative contrast between central and peripheral areas of the visual field underlies the speed overestimation observed with fog, then speed should be underestimated with the anti-fog.
evidence_reasoning: This is a testable hypothesis derived through logical inference from the proposed mechanism.

claim: Ten experienced drivers who had not participated in the first two experiments were tested in the third experiment.
source_text: Ten experienced drivers who had not participated in the first two experiments were presented with pairs of driving scenes and instructed to estimate which scene moved faster
evidence_reasoning: This is a methodological fact about the experimental design and participant sample for experiment 3.

claim: The first two experiments revealed the same pattern of results for all three target speeds.
source_text: Only one target speed was used (60 km/hr) as the first two experiments revealed the same pattern of results for all three target speeds.
evidence_reasoning: This is a summary of findings from experiments 1 and 2 used to justify the design of experiment 3.

claim: Visibility affected perceived speed in experiment 3 with F(2,18) = 28.82, p<0.001, ηG2 = 0.71.
source_text: Visibility affected perceived speed [F(2,18) = 28.82, p<0.001, ηG2 = 0.71].
evidence_reasoning: This is a statistical result from experiment 3 showing a significant main effect of visibility on perceived speed.

claim: As compared to clear visibility, speed was overestimated when visibility was better for close than for distant objects (fog).
source_text: As compared to clear visibility (brown dashed line), speed was overestimated when visibility was better for close than for distant objects, that is, in fog (red bars)
evidence_reasoning: This is a primary finding from experiment 3 supported by PSE measurements in fog conditions.

claim: Speed was underestimated when visibility was better for distant than for close objects (anti-fog).
source_text: and underestimated when visibility was better for distant than for close objects, that is, anti-fog (blue bars).
evidence_reasoning: This is a primary finding from experiment 3 supported by PSE measurements in anti-fog conditions.

claim: All three visibility conditions in experiment 3 differed significantly from one another (p<0.05).
source_text: All three conditions differed significantly from one another (p<0.05).
evidence_reasoning: This is a statistical result from post-hoc tests in experiment 3.

claim: The same 10 participants from experiment 3 took part in experiment 4.
source_text: The same 10 participants took part in a fourth experiment where they were instructed to drive at target speeds with either clear or reduced visibility
evidence_reasoning: This is a methodological fact about the experimental design and participant sample for experiment 4.

claim: Driving speed was affected by visibility in experiment 4 with F(2,18) = 39.99, p<0.001, ηG2 = 0.71.
source_text: Driving speed was affected by visibility [F(2,18) = 39.99, p<0.001, ηG2 = 0.71].
evidence_reasoning: This is a statistical result from experiment 4 showing a significant main effect of visibility on driving speed.

claim: As compared to clear visibility, participants drove slower with fog in experiment 4.
source_text: Specifically, as compared to clear visibility (mean = 67.9 km/hr), participants drove slower with fog (mean = 53.1 km/hr)
evidence_reasoning: This is a primary finding from experiment 4 supported by measured driving speeds in fog conditions.

claim: As compared to clear visibility, participants drove faster with anti-fog in experiment 4.
source_text: and faster with anti-fog (mean = 104.4 km/hr, see Figure 4B).
evidence_reasoning: This is a primary finding from experiment 4 supported by measured driving speeds in anti-fog conditions.

claim: All three visibility conditions in experiment 4 differed from one another (p<0.05).
source_text: All three conditions differed from one another (p<0.05).
evidence_reasoning: This is a statistical result from post-hoc tests in experiment 4.

claim: Visibility affected the variability of driving speed in experiment 4 with F(2,18) = 9.56, p<0.01, ηG2 = 0.33.
source_text: Visibility also affected the variability of driving speed [F(2,18) = 9.56, p<0.01, ηG2 = 0.33]
evidence_reasoning: This is a statistical result from experiment 4 showing a significant effect of visibility on speed variability.

claim: The variability of driving speed was twice as large in the anti-fog condition as in the other two conditions.
source_text: which was twice as large in the anti-fog condition (mean = 17.6 km/hr) as in the other two conditions that did not differ from one another (mean = 9 and 7.5 km/hr for clear visibility and fog, respectively).
evidence_reasoning: This is a finding from experiment 4 comparing speed variability across visibility conditions.

claim: Previous studies suggested that the speed of visual motion in depth is underestimated when the global level of contrast is reduced.
source_text: Previous studies suggested that the speed of visual motion in depth is underestimated when the global level of contrast is reduced (Snowden et al., 1998; Horswill and Plooy, 2008; Owens et al., 2010).
evidence_reasoning: This is a claim about prior research findings, supported by citations to Snowden et al. (1998), Horswill and Plooy (2008), and Owens et al. (2010).

claim: Previous studies on contrast and motion perception were directly inspired by classical vision research experiments that assessed the effect of contrast on the perceived speed of two-dimensional objects on a monitor.
source_text: These studies were directly inspired by classical vision research experiments that assessed the effect of contrast on the perceived speed of two-dimensional objects on a monitor (Thompson, 1982; Stone and Thompson, 1992; Blakemore and Snowden, 1999; Anstis, 2003).
evidence_reasoning: This is a claim about the historical development of research in this area, supported by citations.

claim: The present study reproduced the perceptual bias showing that visual speed is underestimated when contrast is reduced in a distance-independent manner.
source_text: In the present study, we reproduced this perceptual bias, showing that visual speed is indeed underestimated when contrast is reduced in a distance-independent manner.
evidence_reasoning: This is a summary of findings from experiments 1 and 2 confirming prior research with uniform contrast reduction.

claim: An identical global loss of visibility can evoke opposite percepts, depending on the nature of the underlying visual contrast reduction.
source_text: However, we show that this is only part of the whole picture. In particular, we demonstrate here for the first time that an identical global loss of visibility can evoke opposite percepts, depending on the nature of the underlying visual contrast reduction.
evidence_reasoning: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by data from all four experiments showing opposite effects with equal global contrast.

claim: Contrarily to what has been consistently reported in previous studies, a global contrast reduction can also lead to an overestimation of visual speed.
source_text: Therefore, contrarily to what has been consistently reported in previous studies, a global contrast reduction can also lead to an overestimation of visual speed.
evidence_reasoning: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by data showing speed overestimation with distance-dependent contrast reduction.

claim: Global contrast reduction leads to speed overestimation when contrast is not reduced uniformly for all objects of the visual scene but varies according to their distance from the viewer.
source_text: This is notably the case when contrast is not reduced uniformly for all objects of the visual scene but varies according to their distance from the viewer.
evidence_reasoning: This is a primary conclusion supported by data from experiments 1-4 comparing uniform and distance-dependent contrast reduction.

claim: In fog, contrast reduction is more important for distant than for close objects.
source_text: For instance, in fog, contrast reduction is more important for distant than for close objects.
evidence_reasoning: This is a restatement of the physical properties of fog based on established knowledge.

claim: Fog generates a distance-dependent visibility gradient between the peripheral and central area of the visual field.
source_text: This generates a distance-dependent visibility gradient between the peripheral and central area of the visual field.
evidence_reasoning: This is a logical inference about how the distance-dependent properties of fog map onto the visual field during forward motion.

claim: In fog, perceived speed is not determined by the global level of contrast per se, but rather by the spatial distribution of contrast over the visual scene.
source_text: Our results show that in this situation, perceived speed is not determined by the global level of contrast per se, but rather by the spatial distribution of contrast over the visual scene.
evidence_reasoning: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by data showing different perceptual effects with equal global contrast but different spatial distributions.

claim: Perceived speed is determined by the relative contrast between the central and peripheral areas of the visual field.
source_text: More specifically, perceived speed is determined by the relative contrast between the central and peripheral areas of the visual field.
evidence_reasoning: This is a mechanistic conclusion inferred from the pattern of results across all experiments, particularly experiments 3 and 4.

claim: When visibility is better in the peripheral than in the central visual field, as is the case in fog, speed is overestimated.
source_text: When visibility is better in the peripheral than in the central visual field, as is the case in fog, speed is overestimated.
evidence_reasoning: This is a primary finding supported by data from experiments 1-4 showing speed overestimation in fog conditions.

claim: Inverting the direction of the contrast gradient with anti-fog and thereby obscuring more the peripheral than the central region of the visual field, inverts the perceptual bias such that speed is now underestimated.
source_text: Inverting the direction of the contrast gradient with anti-fog and thereby obscuring more the peripheral than the central region of the visual field, inverts the perceptual bias such that speed is now underestimated.
evidence_reasoning: This is a primary finding from experiments 3 and 4 showing speed underestimation in anti-fog conditions.

claim: The results highlight the critical role of the visibility gradient in perceived speed.
source_text: This highlights the critical role of the visibility gradient in perceived speed, explaining why speed is unexpectedly overestimated in fog despite a global reduction of visibility.
evidence_reasoning: This is a conclusion drawn from the pattern of results showing that spatial distribution of contrast matters more than global level.

claim: Speed is unexpectedly overestimated in fog despite a global reduction of visibility.
source_text: explaining why speed is unexpectedly overestimated in fog despite a global reduction of visibility.
evidence_reasoning: This summarizes the key finding that contradicts prior expectations based on uniform contrast reduction studies.

claim: The results evidence the direct relationship between perceived and produced speed.
source_text: Importantly, our results also evidence the direct relationship between perceived and produced speed.
evidence_reasoning: This is a conclusion supported by the consistent correspondence between perceptual judgments (experiments 1 and 3) and driving behavior (experiments 2 and 4).

claim: Speed overestimation systematically prompted drivers to drive slower.
source_text: Specifically, speed overestimation systematically prompted drivers to drive slower, whereas speed underestimation led to faster driving paces.
evidence_reasoning: This is a finding from experiments 2 and 4 showing that perceptual biases directly influenced driving behavior.

claim: Speed underestimation led to faster driving paces.
source_text: Specifically, speed overestimation systematically prompted drivers to drive slower, whereas speed underestimation led to faster driving paces.
evidence_reasoning: This is a finding from experiments 2 and 4 showing that perceptual biases directly influenced driving behavior.

claim: Driving speed is strongly affected by perceived visual speed.
source_text: This demonstrates that driving speed is strongly affected by perceived visual speed.
evidence_reasoning: This is a conclusion drawn from the consistent relationship between perception and behavior across all experiments.

claim: In 'real-life' driving, the roadsides usually include various objects and landmarks as trees, buildings, traffic signs, or pedestrians.
source_text: In 'real-life' driving, the roadsides usually include various objects and landmarks as trees, buildings, traffic signs, or pedestrians.
evidence_reasoning: This is a claim about typical real-world driving environments based on general knowledge.

claim: Objects next to the road can have a cognitive influence on driving speed because they constitute potential obstacles that increase the risk of collision.
source_text: Such objects next to the road can have a cognitive influence on driving speed because they constitute potential obstacles that increase the risk of collision (e.g., tree or building if one drives out of the road and cars or pedestrians suddenly crossing the road).
evidence_reasoning: This is a claim about cognitive factors in driving based on general knowledge about risk perception and driving behavior.

claim: The researchers were interested in the perceptual and not in the cognitive effects of contrast reduction on driving speed.
source_text: However, we were interested in the perceptual and not in the cognitive effects of contrast reduction on driving speed.
evidence_reasoning: This is a statement about the research goals and design rationale.

claim: The roadsides of the driving scenario consisted of a grass texture clear of any object and landmark.
source_text: Therefore, the roadsides of our driving scenario consisted of a grass texture clear of any object and landmark.
evidence_reasoning: This is a methodological fact about the experimental stimulus design.

claim: The absence of landmarks prevented cognitive factors from biasing the results.
source_text: This prevented cognitive factors as those mentioned above to bias our results
evidence_reasoning: This is a claim about the methodological benefit of the design choice, based on logical inference.

claim: The absence of landmarks prevented subjects from using these landmarks to estimate moving speed.
source_text: but importantly, it also prevented subjects of using these landmarks to estimate speed.
evidence_reasoning: This is a claim about the methodological benefit of the design choice, based on logical inference.

claim: Adding landmarks or other 'higher-level' cues would have given the subjects the possibility to use some cognitive strategies to estimate speed.
source_text: Indeed, adding landmarks or other 'higher-level' cues would have given the subjects the possibility to use some cognitive strategies to estimate speed.
evidence_reasoning: This is a speculative claim about what would have happened with a different experimental design, indicated by 'would have'.

claim: Subjects could have used relative size information of landmarks to infer distances and counted passing them to assess speed.
source_text: For instance, subjects could have used relative size information of landmarks to infer distances and counted passing them to assess speed.
evidence_reasoning: This is a speculative claim about potential cognitive strategies, indicated by 'could have'.

claim: Adding landmarks would have biased the results.
source_text: Undoubtedly, this would have biased our results.
evidence_reasoning: This is a speculative claim about the consequences of an alternative design, indicated by 'would have'.

claim: At a 'pure' perceptual level, objects next to the road can contribute to increase peripheral visual flow, thereby altering perceived speed.
source_text: Yet, one could argue that at a 'pure' perceptual level, objects next to the road can also contribute to increase peripheral visual flow, thereby altering perceived speed.
evidence_reasoning: This acknowledges a potential counterargument based on knowledge of visual flow and speed perception.

claim: The effect of roadside objects on peripheral visual flow would be mostly true with a driving environment that provides only little visual flow information.
source_text: This would be mostly true with a driving environment that provides only little visual flow information (e.g., very smooth road pavement and roadsides).
evidence_reasoning: This is a conditional claim based on logical inference about when roadside objects would matter most.

claim: The scene used in the study consisted of a rough asphalt pavement and roughly textured grass roadsides.
source_text: However, the scene we used consisted of a rough asphalt pavement and roughly textured grass roadsides (see Figure 2).
evidence_reasoning: This is a methodological fact about the experimental stimulus design.

claim: The rough textures in the scene provided participants with rich visual flow information when driving.
source_text: These rough textures provided participants with rich visual flow information when driving, as attested by our results.
evidence_reasoning: This is a claim about the stimulus properties supported by inference from the experimental results.

claim: In the 'clear visibility' condition, participants estimated visual speed with great accuracy.
source_text: Specifically, in the 'clear visibility' condition, participants estimated visual speed with great accuracy.
evidence_reasoning: This is a finding from the experiments indicating good performance in baseline conditions.

claim: The variability of speed estimates was small (i.e., low JNDs) in all conditions, and even more with clear visibility.
source_text: In addition, the variability of speed estimates was small (i.e., low JNDs) in all conditions, and even more with clear visibility.
evidence_reasoning: This is a finding from experiments 1 and 3 about discrimination sensitivity across conditions.

claim: The driving scenario provided robust visual flow information allowing for reliable speed estimates.
source_text: Those elements indicate that our driving scenario provided robust visual flow information allowing for reliable speed estimates.
evidence_reasoning: This is a conclusion about the stimulus quality inferred from the accuracy and consistency of participants' performance.

claim: Contrast-dependent modulation of neural activity has been reported at early stages of visual processing, as the retina.
source_text: Contrast-dependent modulation of neural activity has been reported at early stages of visual processing, as the retina (Shapley and Victor, 1978)
evidence_reasoning: This is a claim about neurophysiological findings supported by citation to Shapley and Victor (1978).

claim: Contrast-dependent modulation of neural activity has been reported in the lateral geniculate nucleus.
source_text: Contrast-dependent modulation of neural activity has been reported at early stages of visual processing, as the retina (Shapley and Victor, 1978), the lateral geniculate nucleus (Solomon et al., 2002)
evidence_reasoning: This is a claim about neurophysiological findings supported by citation to Solomon et al. (2002).

claim: Contrast-dependent modulation of neural activity has been reported in the primary visual cortex.
source_text: and the primary visual cortex (Levitt and Lund, 1997; Polat et al., 1998; Sceniak et al., 1999).
evidence_reasoning: This is a claim about neurophysiological findings supported by citations to Levitt and Lund (1997), Polat et al. (1998), and Sceniak et al. (1999).

claim: Contrast-dependent modulation of neural activity has been reported in the middle temporal area (MT or V5).
source_text: It has also been reported in the middle temporal area (MT or V5), an area playing an important role in motion processing (Pack et al., 2005; Bartels et al., 2008)
evidence_reasoning: This is a claim about neurophysiological findings supported by citations to Pack et al. (2005) and Bartels et al. (2008).

claim: The middle temporal area (MT or V5) plays an important role in motion processing.
source_text: the middle temporal area (MT or V5), an area playing an important role in motion processing (Pack et al., 2005; Bartels et al., 2008)
evidence_reasoning: This is a claim about brain function supported by citations and established neuroscience knowledge.

claim: The middle temporal area (MT or V5) plays an important role in speed detection.
source_text: and speed detection (Maunsell and Van Essen, 1983b)
evidence_reasoning: This is a claim about brain function supported by citation to Maunsell and Van Essen (1983b).

claim: MT has feedforward projections to the medial superior temporal area.
source_text: notably via feedforward projections to the medial superior temporal area (Maunsell and van Essen, 1983a; Ungerleider and Desimone, 1986).
evidence_reasoning: This is a claim about neural connectivity supported by citations to Maunsell and van Essen (1983a) and Ungerleider and Desimone (1986).

claim: Linking neurophysiological findings about contrast effects with the effect of contrast on perceived speed in humans is not straightforward.
source_text: Yet, linking these neurophysiological findings with the effect of contrast on perceived speed in humans is not straightforward.
evidence_reasoning: This is an evaluative claim about the difficulty of connecting different levels of analysis, based on the complexity of the relationship.

claim: MT neurons tuned to high speeds are strongly activated by slow stimuli at low contrast.
source_text: For instance, the observation that MT neurons tuned to high speeds are strongly activated by slow stimuli at low contrast (Pack et al., 2005)
evidence_reasoning: This is a claim about neurophysiological findings supported by citation to Pack et al. (2005).

claim: The observation that MT neurons tuned to high speeds are strongly activated by slow stimuli at low contrast would predict speed overestimation at low contrast.
source_text: the observation that MT neurons tuned to high speeds are strongly activated by slow stimuli at low contrast (Pack et al., 2005) would predict speed overestimation at low contrast.
evidence_reasoning: This is a logical inference about what the neurophysiological finding would predict for perception.

claim: The prediction of speed overestimation from MT neuron activity is the opposite of what has been usually observed with uniform contrast reduction.
source_text: This is the opposite of what has been usually observed with uniform contrast reduction, including in the current study.
evidence_reasoning: This identifies an inconsistency between neurophysiological predictions and behavioral observations, supported by data and prior research.

claim: Pack et al. (2005) suggested that the inconsistency between MT neuron activity and perceived speed might be resolved by assuming a bias towards slow speeds when the total MT population activity is low.
source_text: As stated by Pack et al. (2005), this inconsistency might be resolved by assuming a bias towards slow speeds when the total MT population activity is low.
evidence_reasoning: This is a claim about a proposed resolution to the inconsistency, attributed to Pack et al. (2005).

claim: A bias towards slow speed is what is proposed by Bayesian models of speed perception.
source_text: Such a bias towards slow speed is precisely what is proposed by Bayesian models of speed perception (Weiss et al., 2002; Stocker and Simoncelli, 2006).
evidence_reasoning: This is a claim about theoretical models supported by citations to Weiss et al. (2002) and Stocker and Simoncelli (2006).

claim: Bayesian models of speed perception rely on the assumption that speed 'measurements' are intrinsically noisy.
source_text: Specifically, these models rely on the assumption that speed 'measurements' are intrinsically noisy, and that based on our everyday experience, slower motions are more likely to occur than faster ones—resulting in an elevated prior for slow speeds.
evidence_reasoning: This is a claim about the assumptions of Bayesian models, based on the cited literature and general knowledge of Bayesian approaches.

claim: Bayesian models assume that based on our everyday experience, slower motions are more likely to occur than faster ones.
source_text: and that based on our everyday experience, slower motions are more likely to occur than faster ones—resulting in an elevated prior for slow speeds.
evidence_reasoning: This is a claim about the assumptions of Bayesian models regarding natural statistics of motion.

claim: Bayesian models of speed perception can accurately predict speed underestimation at low contrast.
source_text: Whereas Bayesian models of speed perception can accurately predict speed underestimation at low contrast (Stocker and Simoncelli, 2006)
evidence_reasoning: This is a claim about the predictive success of Bayesian models, supported by citation to Stocker and Simoncelli (2006).

claim: Speed overestimation observed at higher speeds is more difficult for Bayesian models to account for.
source_text: speed overestimation observed at higher speeds (Thompson et al., 2006) and at low luminance (Hammett et al., 2007) are more difficult to account for.
evidence_reasoning: This is a claim about limitations of Bayesian models, supported by citations to Thompson et al. (2006) and Hammett et al. (2007).

claim: Speed overestimation observed at low luminance is more difficult for Bayesian models to account for.
source_text: speed overestimation observed at higher speeds (Thompson et al., 2006) and at low luminance (Hammett et al., 2007) are more difficult to account for.
evidence_reasoning: This is a claim about limitations of Bayesian models, supported by citation to Hammett et al. (2007).

claim: Alternative models have proposed that speed is encoded as 'the ratio of the responses of physiologically plausible temporal filters'.
source_text: Alternative models have proposed that speed is encoded as 'the ratio of the responses of physiologically plausible temporal filters' (Hammett et al., 2000; Hammett et al., 2005).
evidence_reasoning: This is a claim about alternative theoretical models, supported by citations to Hammett et al. (2000, 2005).

claim: 'Ratio models' account for both under- and overestimation of speed at low contrast.
source_text: These 'ratio models' account for both under- and overestimation of speed at low contrast (Thompson et al., 2006).
evidence_reasoning: This is a claim about the explanatory power of ratio models, supported by citation to Thompson et al. (2006).

claim: None of the abovementioned models addressed situations in which the amount of contrast reduction differed for different areas of the moving visual scene.
source_text: However, none of the abovementioned models addressed situations in which the amount of contrast reduction differed for different areas of the moving visual scene, as is the case when driving in fog.
evidence_reasoning: This is a claim about limitations of existing models based on review of the literature and the novel aspects of the current study.

claim: Existing models do not explain the differences in speed perception observed with uniform and distance-dependent contrast reduction.
source_text: In that respect, these models do not explain the differences in speed perception observed here with uniform and distance-dependent contrast reduction.
evidence_reasoning: This is a claim about the limitations of existing models in explaining the current findings.

claim: Existing models do not account for opposite biases evoked with the same global contrast reduction at the same actual speed.
source_text: They do not account for opposite biases evoked with the same global contrast reduction at the same actual speed.
evidence_reasoning: This is a claim about the limitations of existing models in explaining the current findings.

claim: Poor visibility conditions affect millions of drivers around the world.
source_text: Poor visibility conditions affect millions of drivers around the world.
evidence_reasoning: This is a claim about the prevalence of the problem based on general knowledge.

claim: Thousands of drivers die each year in a car accident related to poor visibility.
source_text: Thousands of them die each year in a car accident.
evidence_reasoning: This is a claim about traffic fatalities, with 'them' referring to drivers affected by poor visibility conditions, based on general knowledge of traffic safety statistics.

claim: Excessive speed constitutes a major causal factor for car accidents in poor visibility.
source_text: Excessive speed constitutes a major causal factor for these car accidents.
evidence_reasoning: This is a claim about accident causation based on established knowledge in traffic safety research.

claim: The study shows for the first time how fog biases speed perception.
source_text: We show here for the first time how fog biases speed perception
evidence_reasoning: This is a claim about the novelty and contribution of the study, supported by the experimental findings.

claim: The study reveals the perceptual mechanisms underlying the speed bias in fog.
source_text: and we reveal the perceptual mechanisms underlying this bias, providing important insights into the human visual system.
evidence_reasoning: This is a claim about the mechanistic contribution of the study, supported by the experimental findings about spatial distribution of contrast.

claim: The study provides important insights into the human visual system.
source_text: providing important insights into the human visual system.
evidence_reasoning: This is an evaluative claim about the broader significance of the findings for understanding visual perception.

claim: Contrarily to what was previously believed, speed is overestimated in fog because visibility is poorer in the central than in the peripheral area of the visual field.
source_text: In particular, we show that contrarily to what was previously believed, speed is overestimated in fog because visibility is poorer in the central than in the peripheral area of the visual field.
evidence_reasoning: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by data from all experiments, particularly experiments 3 and 4.

claim: The behavioural consequence of speed overestimation in fog is a natural tendency to drive at a slower pace.
source_text: We also show that the behavioural consequence of this speed overestimation is a natural tendency to drive at a slower pace.
evidence_reasoning: This is a finding from experiments 2 and 4 showing that drivers naturally slowed down in fog conditions.

claim: Drivers should probably listen to their visual system when it prompts them to decelerate in fog.
source_text: Therefore, drivers should probably listen to their visual system when it prompts them to decelerate.
evidence_reasoning: This is a practical recommendation based on the findings, with 'probably' indicating some degree of speculation about the appropriate response.

claim: Thirty-two experienced drivers participated voluntarily in the study.
source_text: Thirty-two experienced drivers (23 males and 9 females; aged 21–35 years, mean = 25.3 years) participated voluntarily in the study
evidence_reasoning: This is a methodological fact about the participant sample.

claim: All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
source_text: All had normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
evidence_reasoning: This is a methodological fact about participant inclusion criteria.

claim: The study was performed in accordance with the ethical standards laid down in the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki.
source_text: The study was performed in accordance with the ethical standards laid down in the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki, in line with Max Planck Society policy and in compliance with all relevant German legislation.
evidence_reasoning: This is a statement about the ethical compliance of the research.
